'''Mario Szegedy''' (born October 23, 1960) is a Hungarian and American [[computer scientist]], [[professor]] of [[computer science]] at [[Rutgers University]]. He received his [[Ph.D.]] in computer science in 1989 from the [[University of Chicago]] after completing his dissertation titled ''Algebraic Methods in Lower Bounds for Computational Models''.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=98045}}</ref> He held a [[Lady Davis Fellowship|Lady Davis Postdoctoral Fellowship]] at the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]] (1989–90), a postdoc at the University of Chicago, 1991–92, and a postdoc at [[Bell Labs|Bell Laboratories]] (1992).

Szegedy's research areas include [[computational complexity theory]], [[quantum computing]], [[computational geometry]], and [[computational theory]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Szegedy |first=Mario |title=Szegedy, Mario |url=https://www.cs.rutgers.edu/people/professors/details/mario-szegedy |access-date=2023-12-12 |website=www.cs.rutgers.edu |language=en-gb}}</ref>

He was awarded the [[Gödel Prize]] twice, in 2001 and 2005, for his work on [[probabilistically checkable proof]]s and on the [[space complexity]] of approximating the frequency moments in streamed data.<ref>[http://www.sigact.org/Prizes/Godel/ Gödel Prize website with list of winners]  {{webarchive|url=https://wayback.archive-it.org/all/20161007181643/http://www.sigact.org/Prizes/Godel/ |date=October 7, 2016 }}</ref>  His work on streaming algorithms and the resulting data analysis was also recognized by the 2019 [[Paris Kanellakis Theory and Practice Award]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://awards.acm.org/about/2019-technical-awards|title = ACM announces recipients of three prestigious technical awards for 2019}}</ref> With computer scientists [[Uriel Feige]], [[Shafi Goldwasser]], [[László Lovász]], and [[Shmuel Safra]], Szegedy won the Test of Time Award at the 2021 IEEE Foundations of Computer Science Conference for their work titled ''Approximating Clique is Almost NP-Complete.''

He is married and has two daughters.
